title: Brevard County’s water
lead: Brevard has no single water system. The City of Melbourne, the City of Cocoa, Palm Bay, Titusville and others each run their own drinking-water utilities, and the county’s Utility Services Department runs sewer and some water service in parts of the county. What ties them all together is the Indian River Lagoon — it runs the length of the county, and the county’s stormwater and treated wastewater end up there.

facts.v: Brevard County Utility Services runs sewer service across much of the county, including the south beaches (Melbourne Beach’s sewer, for example). Phone (321) 633-2091.

facts.v: One example: the City of Melbourne — serving about 168,000 people in Melbourne, and the south beaches — draws from Lake Washington (St. Johns River) and the Floridan Aquifer, and is permitted for 25 million gallons a day.

facts.v: City of Melbourne: as of June 8, 2026 its inventory counts 60,726 service lines: 41,789 not lead, 0 lead, 0 galvanized needing replacement, and 18,937 still of unknown material. Each utility keeps its own inventory.

facts.v: From December 2020 to April 2022, 1,255 manatees died in the Indian River Lagoon event, mostly from “starvation due to lack of forage” after the seagrass died off. FWC closed the event in March 2025. Seagrass is coming back: the water management district mapped 17,042 hectares in 2025, up from 9,924 in 2023.

src.label: St. Johns River Water Management District, May 2026

facts.v: Voters approved the Save Our Indian River Lagoon half-cent sales tax in 2016; it pays for muck removal, septic-to-sewer work, stormwater filters and oyster restoration. Its ten-year renewal is on the November 3, 2026 ballot — this site gives facts and takes no side.

State law requires septic systems in the lagoon watershed to connect to sewer or upgrade to nitrogen-reducing systems by 2030. The lagoon program’s septic upgrade cost-share pays $6,000 to $20,000 per property.

quality.lead: Each city utility publishes its own yearly water quality report. The City of Melbourne’s latest (2025 tests) lists one violation: E. coli.

rows.note: No homes over the action level.

quality.violation: E. coli was found in April and May 2025 (“an E. coli positive repeat sample following a total coliform positive routine sample”). The city ran a Level 2 assessment overseen by a third party, which found “no known issues” with the pipes or plants, and installed a dedicated sampling station. A separate August 28, 2025 boil-water notice for all customers was lifted the next day; the city said that result was likely a contaminated sample or lab error.
quality.inspection: July 24, 2026: a taste-and-odor notice after algae in Lake Washington. The city said the water “remains safe to drink” and its tests for algae toxins found none.

fits.name: Clean the rain before it reaches the lagoon
fits.why: Every storm drain in town empties toward the Indian River Lagoon. Filters at the outfalls catch nitrogen and phosphorus — the food for the algae blooms that killed the seagrass.

fits.name: Build on the oyster reefs already here
fits.why: Brevard Zoo’s Restore Our Shores built a 900-square-foot oyster reef at Ryckman Park that drew about 40,000 oysters in a year, and a 965-foot living shoreline on three county conservation lots in town in 2020.

fits.name: Plan for the water that’s coming
fits.why: The town is updating a sea-level and flooding vulnerability study, which is the ticket to state Resilient Florida grants. No Melbourne Beach project appears in the state’s 2025–26 Resilient Florida plan.

question: How many septic systems are left in the lagoon watershed, and how many does the county plan to connect by the state’s 2030 deadline? (Docket #4)

proposal.title: Put a living filter before the lagoon
proposal.summary: Melbourne Beach’s drinking water is already low in byproducts. Its water problem is the other direction: rain carries fertilizer and dirt off streets and lawns, through the town’s pipes, into the lagoon. A living filter at the end of each pipe — an oyster reef, a living shoreline, or a bed of special media where bacteria eat the nitrogen — cleans that water before the lagoon has to. However the drainage work is paid for, it can be built with a living filter at the outfall.

evidence.text: Brevard’s lagoon program builds biosorption activated media (BAM) — an engineered soil mix that removes nitrogen and phosphorus from stormwater. One finished BAM site, Broadway Pond in Port St. John, removes about 456 pounds of nitrogen and 69 pounds of phosphorus a year.

src.label: Save Our Indian River Lagoon — BAM projects

evidence.text: The Ryckman Park oyster reef in Melbourne Beach (900 square feet) drew about 40,000 oysters in a year, and the site now supports more than 20 species. Restore Our Shores reports its newer gabion reefs drew over 40% more live oysters than the old mesh bags.

src.label: Brevard Zoo — Restore Our Shores, oyster reefs

evidence.text: In 2020 Brevard Zoo finished a 965-foot living shoreline — about 17,000 live oysters and more than 3,700 plants of 15 species — on three Brevard environmentally endangered lands properties in Melbourne Beach.

limits: No measured nitrogen numbers were found for the Melbourne Beach reefs or shoreline. Oysters filter water, but how much they clean a given outfall needs testing.
BAM filters need room and upkeep; their media wears out and has to be replaced.
A filter at the pipe doesn’t fix pipes that are broken or too small. It goes with the repairs, not instead of them.
The engineering — where each filter fits and what it costs — belongs to the town’s engineers and the county’s lagoon program.
proposal.why_here: Every city’s storm drains in Brevard empty toward the lagoon. In Melbourne Beach alone, the town describes old, undersized pipes sending rain into the lagoon, and in February 2026 a live manatee had to be removed from a stormwater junction box.

proposal.first_step: Have the lagoon program fund one living-filter pilot per year at a city stormwater outfall — BAM media, an oyster reef, or a living shoreline — with nitrogen tests before and after, and publish the results.
